0.title: The Full Meaning of the Christian Life
0.essay:
Ask a room full of Christians what Christianity is fundamentally about, and many will say: going to heaven when you die. That is not wrong. But it is so much less than the whole.

Not a fire escape

A faith reduced to “believe the right things and avoid hell” produces thin, anxious, self-centred believers who are waiting for life to begin rather than living it now. It produces people who treat this world as a waiting room and their neighbours as projects, and who experience God as a judge to be appeased rather than a Father to be enjoyed.

The biblical vision is far richer. Christianity is about the restoration of the relationship between the living God and the creatures he made to know him — a restoration so complete that we are not merely pardoned but adopted, not merely forgiven but indwelt, not merely saved from something but saved for something. We are saved for God himself: for his glory, for the transformation of our characters into the likeness of his Son, for a real part in his purposes in the world, and finally for a new creation more physical, more beautiful and more alive than anything we have yet known.

A north star

This study is a good place to begin, before the studies on prayer, marriage, suffering and Christian living, because it answers the foundational question: what is all of this for?

It draws on Augustine (“our heart is restless until it rests in you”), the Westminster Shorter Catechism (“Man’s chief end is to glorify God, and to enjoy him forever”), John Piper (“God is most glorified in us when we are most satisfied in him”), C. S. Lewis, Tim Keller and the great stream of Reformed thought that has always insisted that Christianity is not a fire escape. It is a new life, lived to the glory of the one who gave it.

The chapters

Made for God — you were not made for heaven; The Gospel Is Bigger — more than a pardon; To His Glory — the chief end of man; Transformed, Not Just Forgiven; This World Matters; You Are Not Alone; and Glory — the new creation and the resurrection life.

1.title: Made for God: You Were Not Made for Heaven
1.essay:
Here is the great misunderstanding: Christians assume the goal is heaven, and God is the means of getting there. The Bible teaches the opposite. God is the goal. Heaven — the new creation, the resurrection life, the eternal kingdom — is the setting in which we enjoy him fully and for ever.

Joy in a presence

“You make known to me the path of life; in your presence there is fullness of joy; at your right hand are pleasures forevermore” (Psalm 16:11). The psalm places fullness of joy not in a place but in a presence. The pleasures are at his right hand, in his company. That is the Bible’s answer to the human search for lasting satisfaction: it is found in God, not in God’s gifts. Every good gift is better when received from a known and loved Giver, and no gift satisfies when it is made to carry the Giver’s place.

A restless heart

Augustine saw this with unsurpassed clarity. At the very opening of his Confessions, addressing God himself, he wrote: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” Not restless until we reach a place, but until we rest in a Person. The whole human story — the searching, the striving, the longing that no achievement, relationship or pleasure ever fully satisfies — is the echo of a creation made for its Creator.

So every other good thing in life — work, love, beauty, friendship, food, music, laughter — is a signpost, not a destination. These things are real and meant to be enjoyed. But they are enjoyed most fully when received as gifts and allowed to point us to the Giver. C. S. Lewis called this longing “joy”: the inconsolable desire that every pleasure stirs and none can satisfy, which he traced back to its source in the God who made us to know him.

Image-bearers

“So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them” (Genesis 1:27). We are not merely biological organisms but image-bearers, made to know, reflect and relate to the God whose image we bear. The longing no earthly thing can satisfy is the longing of the image for the original. It is not a design flaw; it is the most important fact about being human. And it makes the gospel both necessary and beautiful: the true Image of God has come to bring the image-bearers home.

God did not create us out of need. He is perfectly content in the eternal love of the Trinity. He made us out of overflowing goodness, to share his life, love and glory. The fall did not destroy that purpose; it disrupted it. Redemption does not change the purpose; it restores it.

Eternal life is knowing God

Jesus defined eternal life not as duration but as relationship: “And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3). Eternal life begins the moment someone comes to know God through Christ. And the goal of the whole Christian life is to deepen that knowledge: to know him more fully, love him more completely and be more fully known by him. That is what we were made for and what we are saved for. Everything else serves it.

God with us

The final destination of the biblical story is not souls in a disembodied heaven but God living with his people on a renewed earth: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God” (Revelation 21:3). That has been God’s goal from the garden, where he walked with Adam and Eve (Genesis 3:8), through every covenant — “I will be your God, and you will be my people” — to its final fulfilment. The end is not escape from creation but God’s presence in the middle of it, with his renewed people, for ever.

The man who had everything

A businessman in his mid-fifties has achieved everything he planned: financial security, a good marriage, healthy children, the respect of his peers. Yet he cannot shake the feeling that something is missing. He is not depressed; he is haunted. Lewis would call it the mercy of God: the pleasures meant to point him to God are refusing to be satisfied with less. He comes to faith not because his life has fallen apart but because it has worked and still left him empty. Augustine’s prayer becomes his. He has found what he was made for, and everything else, which was always good, is now better, because he receives it from a known Giver.

For reflection

Have you thought of God as the means and heaven as the goal? What changes if it is the other way round? Which good gift in your life are you tempted to make carry the weight only God can bear? How does John 17:3 change your idea of eternal life?

2.title: The Gospel is Bigger: More Than a Pardon
2.essay:
The minimum version of the gospel goes like this: you have sinned, God is holy, Jesus died to take your punishment; believe in him and you will be forgiven and go to heaven when you die. Every word is true. But it is to the gospel what a seed catalogue is to a garden: accurate, and utterly inadequate to the reality.

Every spiritual blessing

“Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 1:3). Not some blessings, not the most important ones, but every one, and all of them “in Christ”. The list that follows through Ephesians 1–3 is overwhelming: chosen, predestined, adopted, redeemed, forgiven, sealed, given the Spirit as a guarantee, made alive, raised, seated, created for good works, brought near, indwelt.

The New Testament’s vocabulary for what God has done is breathtaking. We are forgiven. We are justified, declared righteous with Christ’s righteousness. We are adopted into God’s family with all the rights of children. We are reconciled, the enmity ended. We are redeemed, bought back from slavery at the price of Christ’s blood. We are born again, given a new nature by the Spirit, and indwelt by the Spirit himself. We are united with Christ, so that his death is our death, his resurrection our resurrection, his righteousness our righteousness. God has “seated us with him in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 2:6). We are “fellow heirs with Christ” (Romans 8:17).

Each is a facet of the same diamond. Someone who knows only “I am forgiven” has seen the diamond but not yet turned it in the light. Forgiveness is the door. Inside the house are rooms many believers have never entered.

The room of adoption

“For you did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’” (Romans 8:15). J. I. Packer called adoption the highest privilege the gospel offers. We are not God’s employees, tolerated on good behaviour, but his beloved sons and daughters, with all the closeness, security and inheritance that implies. “Abba” is a child’s word for a father — warm, close, trusting — and the Spirit enables us to address the Creator of the universe with it. That is not presumption; it is the gift.

A woman who has been a Christian for twenty years thinks of herself mainly as “a forgiven sinner”. She is grateful but always guilty, conscious of her failures, never at ease in God’s presence. Her pastor opens Romans 8:15–16 with her. She has been living in the servants’ quarters when she had the rights of a daughter all along. Adoption, discovered not as a category but as a reality, changes her prayers, her sense of who she is and her relationship with God. She begins to pray as a daughter, not a defendant.

The room of new creation

“Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come” (2 Corinthians 5:17). Not reformed, not improved, not cleaned up, but new. The person in Christ has not turned over a new leaf; they have been given a new life. That is why the Christian life is not first about moral improvement. It is about becoming what you already are.

The room of union

“I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). It is the most intimate picture of union with Christ in the Gospels. A branch does not produce fruit by effort; it bears fruit by remaining in the vine and drawing its life. The Christian life is not performance but abiding, and the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23) is not achieved but produced by Christ’s life flowing through us. “Apart from me you can do nothing” is not a rebuke but a relief. We were never meant to do it alone.

The key to the house

The Reformation’s five solas describe the scope of the gospel. But union with Christ is the architectural key to the whole building. Calvin called justification “the main hinge on which religion turns”, and he insisted that we receive it only as we are joined to Christ. Because we are united to him by faith through the Spirit, his righteousness is credited to us (justification), his life flows into us (sanctification), his Spirit is given to us (adoption and indwelling), and his future is guaranteed to us (glorification). Every blessing of the gospel is an outworking of one reality: we are in Christ, and Christ is in us.

That fullness changes not only our eternal destination but our present experience of God.

For reflection

Which room of the gospel have you lived in most, and which have you hardly entered? Read Ephesians 1:3–14 and list every blessing “in Christ”. Do you pray more like a defendant or a child? What does John 15:5 lift off your shoulders?

3.title: To His Glory: The Chief End of Man
3.essay:
The Westminster Shorter Catechism opens with the most important question a human being can ask: “What is the chief end of man?” Its answer may be the finest sentence written outside Scripture: “Man’s chief end is to glorify God, and to enjoy him forever.”

Glorify and enjoy

Not glorify God instead of enjoying him. Not enjoy him after we have finished glorifying him. Both together, at once, for ever. This is the north star of the Christian life. Every decision, relationship and use of time, money and energy, every moment of suffering and every moment of joy, is to be oriented to this one magnificent purpose. Not as a burden but as a freedom. Whoever has found their chief end has found what makes everything else make sense. They no longer have to write their own story; they get to play their part in the greatest story ever told.

John Piper, building on Jonathan Edwards, put it this way: “God is most glorified in us when we are most satisfied in him.” Glorifying God is not a grim duty done alongside the real business of enjoying life. It is the deepest enjoyment. When we find in God our greatest treasure and highest joy, we glorify him most fully. Edwards saw the glory of God and the happiness of his creatures as a single overflowing reality. God is not glorified despite our joy but through it.

Whatever you do

“So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31). The examples are deliberately ordinary. If even eating and drinking can glorify God, nothing is left out. The Christian life is not divided into sacred and secular, the Sunday sermon and the Monday meeting. All of it, done consciously in dependence on God, in gratitude to him and in reflection of his character, is worship. That is one of the most liberating truths in Christian ethics: not a longer list of religious duties, but ordinary life transfigured into praise.

A young teacher wonders whether her work matters to God. She is not a pastor or missionary; she teaches mathematics to teenagers in a state school. A mentor shows her 1 Corinthians 10:31, and Luther’s teaching on vocation: every honest calling done with excellence and love is worship. She begins to teach differently — not less rigorously, but with a new awareness. Every student she serves well is a neighbour loved in Christ’s name. Every lesson prepared with care is an offering. Every moment of patience with a struggling student reflects God’s patience with her. Her classroom has become a sanctuary — not because she has stopped teaching mathematics, but because she has understood what it is for.

The creature at its most human

“All the nations you have made shall come and worship before you, O Lord, and shall glorify your name” (Psalm 86:9). The psalm looks ahead to the day when people from every background bring their glory to God. The Catechism’s answer is not an arbitrary religious demand. It describes what human beings look like when they are fully themselves and fully alive. The worshipping creature is the creature at its most human.

Lives that point beyond us

“In the same way, let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16). Good works done rightly are not self-promotion; they lead others to praise not us but our Father. Our lives become transparent to him. The love we show, the integrity we keep, the peace we carry through suffering point beyond us to the one who produced them. “For we are the aroma of Christ to God” (2 Corinthians 2:15).

To live is Christ

Paul compressed the whole Christian life into one line: “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21). Not “to live is to follow Christ’s example”, but “to live is Christ”. His whole existence had been reoriented around a Person. Christ was not a compartment of his life but its content and centre. And because to live is Christ, to die is gain: death brings more of him, not less. Even death becomes worship.

Not a threat to our good

The glory of God runs through every major Reformed confession — Westminster, Heidelberg, Belgic. But God’s glory is not a threat to human flourishing; it is its condition. The God who is glorified in our joy, love, creativity, work and worship is the God who designed us for them. His glory and our good are not rivals. They are one.

For reflection

How would you answer the Catechism’s first question in your own words? Where do you still divide your life into sacred and secular? What ordinary task this week could you do consciously “to the glory of God”? What would it mean for you to say, “to live is Christ”?

4.title: Transformed, Not Just Forgiven: Becoming Like Christ
4.essay:
Justification is God’s declaration: you are righteous in his sight because of Christ. It is complete, instantaneous and irreversible. But it is not the whole of salvation. Alongside it runs sanctification, the lifelong work by which the Spirit transforms the justified person into the actual likeness of Jesus.

The goal: Christlikeness

God does not merely declare us righteous; he is making us righteous. He does not merely pardon our character; he is changing it. Romans 8:29 names the goal: we are predestined “to be conformed to the image of his Son”. The word means sharing the same form or shape. The aim of the Christian life is not moral improvement or religious performance but Christlikeness: thinking as he thought, loving as he loved, serving as he served, suffering as he suffered, rejoicing as he rejoiced. That is a staggering ambition, and it is God’s ambition for every believer without exception.

The destination of election is a family of people who look like Jesus — not a slightly better version of our present selves, but his full likeness. It is a lifetime’s work, and Paul describes its goal as “mature manhood … the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Ephesians 4:13). Nothing less. But it is God’s determined purpose, so he will see it through in every one of his people.

We work, and God works

The process is neither automatic nor passive. “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:12–13). That is the great paradox of sanctification. “Work out” means active, serious effort. “With fear and trembling” means earnest, not casual. And underneath it all is God, working in us. We are not straining to meet a standard in our own strength; we are cooperating with a power already at work within us. It is not passivity but active dependence, the most energetic form of trust.

The means are the ordinary means of grace — Scripture, prayer, the Lord’s Supper, fellowship and even suffering — through which the Spirit does his work. Sanctification is not striving to become acceptable to God. It is cooperating with the Spirit as he makes us more like the Son whom God already loves.

Changed by beholding

“And we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another” (2 Corinthians 3:18). Transformation happens through beholding. Its primary means is not moral effort but steady contemplation of the glory of Christ — in Scripture, prayer, worship and the Lord’s Supper. The pace is gradual, “from one degree of glory to another”; the direction is certain; and the agent is the Spirit. Someone who wants to grow in Christlikeness should ask not first “What must I do?” but “Am I truly beholding him?”

We shall be like him

“Beloved, we are God’s children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). The principle of 2 Corinthians 3:18 reaches its fulfilment: the full, face-to-face sight of Christ will make us fully like him. Until then we are God’s children now — the identity secure, the process incomplete, the destination certain. Already children, not yet fully like him: that is the normal Christian experience.

Distinct but inseparable

Reformed theology keeps justification and sanctification distinct but inseparable. Justification is legal, instantaneous and complete; sanctification is transforming, progressive and unfinished until glory. Yet the chain is unbroken: “those whom he justified he also glorified” (Romans 8:30). Calvin wrote that we cannot possess Christ for righteousness “without being made partaker in his sanctification, because he cannot be divided into pieces.” Justification without sanctification would be a legal fiction; sanctification without justification would be salvation by works. Together they are the full salvation of the gospel.

The right combatant

A man has been a Christian for thirty years and is discouraged. He expected to be further along by now — less angry, less proud, more patient, more loving. He feels like a failure. His pastor sits with him and says: “The fact that you see these things — the anger, the pride — is itself evidence of the Spirit’s work. Someone who cannot see their sin is in a more dangerous place than someone who can. Sanctification is not a straight line; it is a battle, and the battlefield is proof that the war is real.” Then he shows him 2 Corinthians 3:18: “from one degree of glory to another”. One degree at a time, and not by the man’s striving alone, but by the Spirit. The discouragement lifts — not because the battle is over, but because the right combatant is fighting it.

For reflection

Have you thought of salvation mainly as forgiveness or as transformation? How do Philippians 2:12–13 hold together your effort and God’s work? What would it look like to “behold” Christ more this week? Where do you need the pastor’s encouragement that seeing your sin is a sign of life?

5.title: This World Matters: Salt, Light, and the Renewal of Creation
5.essay:
One of the most damaging distortions of Christianity is the idea that this world is a burning building from which souls must be rescued before it is destroyed. On that view, culture, work, art, politics and care for creation are at best distractions and at worst idolatries. That is not the biblical view.

Very good, and being renewed

God made this world and saw that “it was very good” (Genesis 1:31). He became flesh and lived in it (John 1:14). He is reconciling all things to himself in Christ. And the final destination of the story is not the destruction of creation but its renewal: “a new heaven and a new earth” (Revelation 21:1), not the annihilation of the old but its transformation. The one on the throne says, “Behold, I am making all things new” (Revelation 21:5) — all things new, not all new things.

Herman Bavinck put it in three words: grace restores nature. The redemption Christ brings does not destroy the created order; it heals, renews and glorifies it. So the work of the painter, the teacher, the doctor, the parent and the builder, done to God’s glory, is not wasted. In some transformed way it is gathered up into the new creation.

All things

“For in him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell, and through him to reconcile to himself all things, whether on earth or in heaven, making peace by the blood of his cross” (Colossians 1:19–20). The scope of Christ’s reconciling work is cosmic, not only personal. This is not universalism. It means that the redemption Christ accomplished reaches beyond the individual heart to the whole created order. The Christian who works for justice, beauty, truth and human flourishing is not doing something separate from the gospel; they are moving in the direction the whole creation is heading.

The cultural mandate

At the beginning God told humanity, “Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth and subdue it” (Genesis 1:28): to fill, cultivate and steward the earth as his image-bearers. That calling has never been revoked. The fall distorted it; Christ restores and reorients it. The redeemed take it up again, freed from sin’s rule, empowered by the Spirit, working not for self-importance but for God’s glory and their neighbour’s good. Every honest calling — farmer, scientist, artist, parent, governor — shares in that original vocation. The Christian doctor, teacher, artist, entrepreneur and parent are not doing second-rate kingdom work.

Salt and light

“You are the salt of the earth … You are the light of the world” (Matthew 5:13–14). Salt preserves and flavours; light shows the way. Both describe engagement with the world, not withdrawal from it. Salt works by contact: it must be in the meat, not the salt cellar. Light works by presence: it must be in the darkness, not in a room full of other lights. A Christian community that withdraws to protect its purity has misunderstood both pictures. Jesus prayed not that the Father would take his people out of the world, but that he would keep them from the evil one (John 17:15).

Every act of real human flourishing — justice done, beauty made, truth told, love shown, the poor fed, the sick healed — is a foretaste of the new creation.

Not a square inch

Common grace — God’s goodness to all people, not only to his chosen — and the cultural mandate together ground Christian engagement with the world. Abraham Kuyper gave the Reformed tradition its battle cry: “There is not a square inch in the whole domain of our human existence over which Christ, who is Sovereign over all, does not cry: Mine!” Christ’s lordship is not limited to the church. The Reformation heritage has borne rich fruit in the arts (Bach, Rembrandt), in politics (Wilberforce), in education and in social reform. That is not a distraction from the gospel; it is the gospel’s fruit.

An architect’s worship

A Christian architect designs affordable housing for a low-income community. She does not think of it as her “secular job” alongside her “real” Christian life. It is her vocation, her calling from God to use her gifts for her neighbours and for the flourishing of God’s world. The families who move into well-designed, dignified homes are experiencing, in a small but real way, the justice and beauty of the new creation. When people ask why she does it, she speaks of a God who became poor so that others might be rich, and who cares about the bodily and social flourishing of those who bear his image. Her work is her witness. Her architecture is her worship.

For reflection

Have you thought of the world as a burning building or as a creation being renewed? What difference does “all things new” make to your work? Where are you called to be salt and light — in contact, not withdrawn? What “square inch” of your life have you not yet handed over to Christ?

6.title: You Are Not Alone: The Body, the Family, the Holy Nation
6.essay:
Western Christianity has produced something the New Testament does not recognise: the solo Christian. Someone who “has their faith” as a private possession, who may attend church now and then, but whose Christian life is essentially a personal transaction between themselves and God. That person has misread the whole shape of the New Testament.

No Christian alone

The New Testament knows no Christian outside a community. From Pentecost on, Jesus’ followers were defined by their shared life: teaching, praying and eating together, sharing possessions and meeting needs (Acts 2:42–47). Its main pictures of the church are all irreducibly corporate: a body (you cannot be a detached limb), a family (you cannot be a solitary child), a temple of living stones fitted together, a holy nation. And its “one another” commands — love one another, serve one another, bear one another’s burdens, confess to one another, forgive one another — cannot be obeyed alone.

That is not only a sociological observation but a theological one. God himself is a communion — Father, Son and Holy Spirit in eternal relationship. He made us in his image, for relationship. He saved us into a community. And he will bring us to glory together.

The body of Christ

“Now you are the body of Christ and individually members of it” (1 Corinthians 12:27). Paul does not say the church is like a body; he says it is the body of Christ, the form in which the risen Christ is present in the world, his hands and feet, his voice and embrace. So when the body fails — when members withdraw, love is absent and the lonely are left alone — it is not only a social failure but a theological one. The world is deprived of a sight of Christ it cannot get any other way.

Bearing burdens

“Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2). The law of Christ is his command to love one another as he has loved us (John 13:34), and it is fulfilled in burden-bearing. Not advice-giving or fixing, though those have their place, but getting under the weight someone else carries and sharing it. That takes presence more than solutions, time more than efficiency, and a willingness to be inconvenienced. It is Christ’s love made visible in his body.

A man goes through a severe depression. His instinct is to withdraw from church, friends and the small group he has attended for years. A couple from the group refuse to let him disappear. They call. They visit. They bring food. They sit in silence with him when he cannot talk. They offer no easy answers. They stay. Years later he says, “The church was the means of my survival. Not because they said the right things — they often didn’t. But because they stayed.” That is the body working as designed: bearing burdens, weeping “with those who weep” (Romans 12:15), refusing to let a member suffer alone. The theology of the body, made flesh in a Tuesday-night visit.

A drama before the universe

Ephesians 1–3 unfolds the cosmic mystery of the gospel, and its climax is the church: “so that through the church the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 3:10). The wisdom of the cross, of grace, of reconciling enemies into a family, is displayed to the spiritual powers of the universe through the visible life of the church. When a church loves across racial, economic and social lines, forgives instead of retaliating, and welcomes the weak and the poor, it is performing before the watching universe a drama that shows the wisdom of God.

So the church is not an add-on to the gospel; it is part of its content. A diverse community of people from every background, living in genuine love, is itself a proclamation of the gospel. The church is not merely a means to something else; it is part of what God is doing in the world.

A choir, not a solo

The final community is “a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb” (Revelation 7:9). That is where the church’s shared life is heading: not isolated individuals drifting into a private heaven, but a vast, diverse, united multitude worshipping together. The local church, with all its imperfections and frustrations, is the earthly anticipation of that reality. Every Sunday gathering is a rehearsal for the great day; every act of cross-cultural love in a congregation is a foretaste of the world to come.

The Christian life is not a solo performance. It is a choir, and each voice needs the others.

For reflection

In what ways have you treated your faith as a private possession? Whose burden could you help carry this week, by presence more than advice? What does Ephesians 3:10 say about the importance of your church’s ordinary life together? Who in your church needs you to “stay”?

7.title: Glory: The New Creation and the Resurrection Life
7.essay:
The Christian hope is not the immortality of the soul. It is the resurrection of the body. It is not escape from this world but the renewal of this world: embodied people, with glorified, physical, recognisable bodies, living in a renewed creation with the God who made them, among the redeemed of all ages, in a joy that has no shadow of ending.

Why it matters now

If the final destination were a disembodied, ethereal heaven, then this world — our bodies, relationships, work and culture — would be ultimately disposable. But if it is a renewed creation in which everything done in Christ’s name has its place, then what we do now has weight and permanence. Paul says so directly, at the end of his great chapter on the resurrection: “Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain” (1 Corinthians 15:58). The prayer prayed, the child discipled, the justice pursued, the beauty made, the poor served, the gospel proclaimed — none of it evaporates.

The resurrection body

“So is it with the resurrection of the dead. What is sown is perishable; what is raised is imperishable. It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power. It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body” (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). “Sown” implies continuity: it is the same body, transformed. A “spiritual body” is not a non-physical body, but one fully animated by the Spirit, no longer subject to decay, disease or death. Jesus’ risen body is the prototype: physical enough to eat (Luke 24:43), solid enough to be touched (John 20:27), yet free of the old limits. That is what awaits every believer — not a ghost, but a glorified, embodied, fully alive self. “But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20).

Labour pains

Creation itself “will be set free from its bondage to corruption and obtain the freedom of the glory of the children of God. For we know that the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now. And not only the creation, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies” (Romans 8:21–23). The groaning of creation is labour pain, not a death rattle. It is in the anguish of bringing something new to birth. And we groan with it, not in despair but in eager longing, because the Spirit is the firstfruits that tell us what the harvest will be. The body itself will be redeemed, not discarded.

More, not less

The glory to come is not less than what we have now but more: more physical, more alive, more relational. It is the difference between a picture of a meal and the meal itself, between a description of a sunrise and the sunrise. Everything beautiful, true and good we know now is a shadow of what will be. The music we have heard is a few notes of the symphony. The love we have known is a glimpse of the Love that is its source. The joy we have tasted is the first sip from a cup that will never run dry.

Every tear

The end of the story is God living with his people: the covenant promise — “I will be their God, and they will be my people” — reaching its final fulfilment. “He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away” (Revelation 21:4). Personally, tenderly, with his own hand. Every loss, every injustice, every unanswered question is met by the God who was there through all of it. And then: “Behold, I am making all things new” (Revelation 21:5). Not some things. All things.

Reformed eschatology is robustly physical. The Westminster Confession affirms the bodily resurrection of all people and the last judgment, and Scripture adds the promise of new heavens and a new earth; Anthony Hoekema’s The Bible and the Future sets out the biblical vision in full. The new creation is not the replacement of this one but its transformation: the healing of what was broken, the glorifying of what was good, the removal of all that corrupts. It is not a return to Eden but Eden glorified, because the last Adam has done what the first failed to do.

Worth going to

An elderly woman dying of cancer asks her pastor, “What will it actually be like?” He does not reach for platitudes. He opens Revelation 21–22 and reads. He talks about a city with no temple, because God himself is its temple; no night, because he is its light; the tree of life bearing fruit every month; the nations bringing their glory into it, the best of human culture purified and offered to God; the river of life, the throne, the Lamb. She listens with her eyes closed. When he finishes she says, “That sounds like something worth going to.” She dies six weeks later with what her family call an extraordinary peace.

The theology of glory is not an abstract doctrine. It is a pastoral necessity, and for the dying it is everything. This is the final answer to the question of what Christianity is all about: a life — this life, every ordinary moment of it — lived in the light of a resurrection that has already happened and a new creation that is already on its way. Labour in the Lord. It is not in vain.

For reflection

Have you pictured eternity as disembodied? What changes if it is a renewed, physical creation? Which of your ordinary labours does 1 Corinthians 15:58 encourage you about? Read Revelation 21–22 slowly. What do you most long for there?
